nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
1994 Jan 1. REB|RGG; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution
Note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Lined Sole
Scientific Name:  Achirus lineatus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Pleuronectiformes
	Family:  Soleidae

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Linnaeus 1758)
	Reference for Classification (1914)
	Revision dates should be checked

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  None
Recreational:  None
Ecological:   Adults are common on continental shelves adjacent to the Florida peninsula, while juveniles are abundant to common in estuaries (2420; 848, 993).  Juveniles make nocturnal surface migrations with flood tides into tidal creeks and the perimeter ditches of impounded red mangrove forests (2417).  Because they spend time in a variety of habitats, it is likely that they are a vector for biological transport of energy/productivity among habitats.
Indicator:  None known

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  The lined sole is found in the western Atlantic from Florida to Uruguay and throughout the Gulf of Mexico (887; 2414; 2420).
Within Study Area:  The lined sole is found throughout the Indian River Lagoon (1889; 1814; 887; 848; 2320).
Life Mode:   The lined sole is a euryhaline, epibenthic species found in a variety of habitats (2415; 664; 848; 327).
Mobility and Migration: The size distribution mentioned above indicates that as this sole matures, it may move into more saline waters.  A second movement pattern was observed by Gilmore et al. (1986).  They observed juvenile nocturnal surface migrations through culverts connecting impounded mangrove forests on South Hutchinson Island to the Indian River Lagoon.  Of the 122 individuals collected in the culverts, only 2 were longer than 30 mm SL (38 and 52 mm; Gilmore unpub. data).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body: The lined sole can be found within the Indian River Lagoon in tributaries, canals, wetlands, inlets, and open lagoon habitats, i.e. seagrass or mangrove lined tidal ditches and creeks.  It can also be found offshore on sand bottoms (1889; 1814; 887; 848, 1988; 2320; 2417).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body: This species is generally restricted to sand or mud substrates, sometimes with high organic content or shell fragments (1889; 848, 1988; 2419; 2417).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity: The lined sole has been collected in the Indian River Lagoon system in salinities ranging from <1 to 33.5 ppt (1889; 1814; 887).  It has also been found in full seawater offshore (2420; 848).  This species may be distributed by size along a salinity gradient with younger smaller individuals being found in lower salinities (255; 587).
Temperature: This species has been collected in inshore habitats in temperatures ranging from 11.2 to 33 C (587; 664; 887).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  The lined sole is a sexually dimorphic, gonochoristic, oviparous, polygamous, broadcast spawner, and is iteroparous ({family Soleidae, 1915}; 2418; 2301).
Mating/Spawning: The lined sole spawns inshore (2416; 2420) April to November in Tampa Bay with maximum catch in June and July, but may start earlier in Florida Bay (2416)
Fecundity: No information. (Related Trinectes maculatus {=Achirus fasciatus Lacepede} can carry 54,000 eggs {1915})

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  This species produces pelagic spherical eggs average 0.74 mm (0.71-0.76 mm) in diameter with multiple oil globules (2418, 2301).
Larvae:  Laboratory raised larvae are about 1.59 mm SL 6 hours after hatching.  They begin to feed after their eyes were pigment and yolk absorbed about 40 hrs after hatching (1.9 mm SL).  Ten days after hatching at an averages size between 3.0 and 3.2 mm SL metamorphosis begins (2418).  During this period, the left eye migrates across the midline to the right side of the head.  Metamorphosis is complete by about 5 mm SL (2418, 2301).  The left pectoral fin disappears after transformation (2301).
Juvenile:  At approximately 10 mm SL, young are considered juveniles (2416; 2418).  Swimbladders, which become reduced during metamorphosis, are absent in juveniles (2418).  In laboratory experiments, 20 specimens averaged 37.5 mm SL at 200 days.  Specimens as large as 61 mm SL were still considered juveniles by Houde et al. (1970).
Adult:  Age at maturity is not available, however samples collected on the Hourglass cruises indicated that specimens ranging in size from 78 to 85 mm SL had eggs in various stages of ripening (2420).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Information on juvenile and adult feeding habits of the lined sole is sparse.  One study showed that food in a limited number of specimens primarily consisted of polychaetes and gammarids (664), while a second study found shell fragments and crustacean parts in one specimen (2420).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Adults are common on continental shelves adjacent to the Florida peninsula, while juveniles are abundant in estuaries (2420; 848, 1988).  Juveniles make nocturnal surface migrations with flood tides into tidal creeks and the perimeter ditches of impounded red mangrove forests (2417).  Because it spends time in a variety of habitats, it is likely a vector for biological transport of energy/productivity among habitats.
